points.title: Repetition (重複)/Synonymy / Near-Synonymy(同義詞/近義詞)/Antonymy (反義詞)
examples: 在篇章中,為使主題貫穿全文,主題字彙會不斷出現,常見的手法有: 原詞重複，讓主題更鮮明
同義詞/近義詞：增加變化性，在語意上相互補充。
除了多次出現與主題意義相同或相近的字詞外,也常常出現與主題意義相反或對比的字詞。雖為反義詞,實質上仍圍繞著同一主題並加以闡述,因此有助於強化篇章的連貫性。

items.sentence: Fake news *can be defined* as news containing false or misleading information that appears truthful.
items.pattern: S + Vt (Passive) + Prepositional phrase + Relative clause / Participle modifier

items.sentence: Although fake news has long been in existence and this issue is as old as the news industry itself, the Internet and social media *have made* creating and sharing fake news easier and faster than ever.
items.pattern: Adverbial clause (Although...) + S + Vt + O + OC

items.sentence: People *may be deceived* by fake news, believing the content to be genuine without questioning the sources.
items.pattern: S + Vt (Passive) + Participle phrase

items.sentence: With so much fake news being spread every day, it *is* now more important than ever to understand where such news comes from and to question the news stories we read.
items.pattern: Prepositional phrase (With...) + It (Formal S) + Vi + C + Infinitive clause + Noun clause

items.sentence: Fake news *comes* in many forms, but two types *are* the most common.
items.pattern: Compound sentence (with "but")

items.sentence: First, fake news *can come* from sloppy journalism, which occurs when journalists write stories based on unreliable information or without fact-checking their sources prior to publication.
items.pattern: S + Vi + Non-restrictive Relative clause + Adverbial clause (when...)

items.sentence: Second, some news *contains* deliberately false information to achieve social or political goals; examples *include* attempts to influence people to vote for a certain candidate or support a particular cause.
items.pattern: S + Vt + O + Infinitive phrase ; S + Vt + O

items.sentence: The following example *illustrates* the potential long-lasting consequences of spreading false information.
items.pattern: S + Vt + O

items.sentence: In 1998, a British researcher *published* a small-scale study in a respected medical journal.
items.pattern: Prepositional phrase + S + Vt + O + Prepositional phrase

items.sentence: The study *claimed* a link between the MMR vaccine and autism.
items.pattern: S + Vt + O + Prepositional phrase

items.sentence: The media *provided* extensive coverage of this flawed study, leading to the widespread belief that the vaccine could cause autism.
items.pattern: S + Vt + O + participle phrase + Appositive clause (that...)

items.sentence: As a result, public confidence in the vaccine *was shattered*, and vaccination rates *declined*.
items.pattern: Compound sentence (with "and")

items.sentence: However, subsequent studies with larger samples *revealed* different findings, and the original study *was eventually proved* inaccurate.
items.pattern: Compound sentence (with "and")

items.sentence: Despite this, misleading details from the initial study *have continued* to spread for years.
items.pattern: Prepositional phrase (Despite...) + S + Vt + Infinitive phrase

items.sentence: Some parents thus *have refused* to vaccinate their children for fear that it might do more harm than good.
items.pattern: S + Vt + O + Prepositional phrase + Noun clause (that...)

items.sentence: More than two decades *have now passed* since the original study was published, but its effects *can still be observed* worldwide.
items.pattern: Adverbial clause (since...) + Compound sentence (with "but")

items.sentence: Another example *shows* how companies manipulate the news for their own advantage.
items.pattern: S + Vt + Noun clause (how...)

items.sentence: On February 23, 2018, a major hypermarket in Taiwan *sent* an email to several media outlets, exaggerating an upcoming increase in the price of toilet paper.
items.pattern: S + Vt + O + participle phrase

items.sentence: It *was later found* that the retailer’s true intention in doing so was merely to advertise its own toilet paper promotion, but by noon that day, the damage *had already been done*.
items.pattern: It (Formal S) + Noun clause (that...) + Compound sentence (with "but")

items.sentence: Two mainstream media outlets *reported* on the imminent price hike without fact-checking, and others soon *followed* suit.
items.pattern: Compound sentence (with "and")

items.sentence: The reporting *prompted* a wave of panic buying among Taiwanese people, many of whom feared that if they didn’t stock up, they would run out of the precious daily necessity.
items.pattern: S + Vt + O + Non-restrictive Relative clause + Adverbial clause (if...)

items.sentence: Even manufacturers *were negatively impacted*, as their factories had to work overtime to handle the sudden increase in demand.
items.pattern: S + Vi (Passive) + Adverbial clause (as...)

items.sentence: These events *remind* us that we must remain alert to fake news.
items.pattern: S + Vt + O + Noun clause (that...)

items.sentence: Whenever we come across new information, it *is* essential to evaluate its validity so that we do not mistake fake news for the truth.
items.pattern: Adverbial clause (Whenever...) + It (Formal S) + Adverbial clause (so that...)

items.sentence: One notable feature of reliable reporting *is* the inclusion of the writer’s name, which allows readers to view that writer’s biography and verify his or her credibility.
items.pattern: S + Vi + C + Non-restrictive Relative clause

items.sentence: Another important sign *is* whether the article cites multiple primary sources, a practice that supports its trustworthiness.
items.pattern: S + Vi + Noun clause (whether...) + Appositive phrase + Relative clause

items.sentence: It *is* also worth considering where the article was published, since respected media platforms such as the BBC or CNN tend to provide dependable coverage.
items.pattern: It (Formal S) + Gerund phrase + Noun clause + Adverbial clause (since...)

items.sentence: Last but not least, factual reports *are usually written* in an objective manner that avoids emotional manipulation and provocative language.
items.pattern: S + Vi (Passive) + Relative clause (that...)

items.sentence: By paying attention to these features, we *can reduce* the risk of falling for fake news.
items.pattern: Prepositional phrase (By...) + S + Vt + O

items.sentence: In the current age of news overload, we *must all watch out* for fake news lest we fall victim to it.
items.pattern: Prepositional phrase + S + Vi + Adverbial clause (lest...)

items.sentence: Useful strategies *include* thinking critically about what we are reading and conducting further research on news stories to check their content before accepting them as truth.
items.pattern: S + Vt + Gerund phrase + Noun clause + Adverbial clause (before...)

items.sentence: With due diligence, we *can win* the war against fake news and *help* improve society.
items.pattern: Prepositional phrase (With...) + S + Vt (Compound verb) + O

text_genre.raw_text:
The text follows a classic Problem-Solution expository framework:
Paragraph 1 — Definition & Problem (Background)
Definition: Fake news is false or misleading information presented as truth.
Context: Social media and the Internet accelerate its spread, deceiving readers who fail to verify sources.
Paragraph 2 — Root Causes (Origins)
Cause 1 (Sloppy Journalism): Unintentional spread due to poor fact-checking by journalists.
Cause 2 (Deliberate Manipulation): Intentional creation of false stories to achieve political or social goals.
Paragraphs 3 & 4 — Real-World Examples (Consequences)
Example 1 (Public Health): The flawed 1998 MMR vaccine study caused long-term fears and declining vaccination rates worldwide.
Example 2 (Economic Panic): A 2018 Taiwan retailer exaggerated price hikes, triggering panic buying and supply chain disruptions.
Paragraph 5 — Solutions & Criteria (Evaluation)
Criterion 1 (Author Credibility): Look for writer bylines and verifiable biographies.
Criterion 2 (Source Diversity): Ensure the report cites multiple primary sources.
Criterion 3 (Platform Reputation): Rely on established media (e.g., BBC, CNN).
Criterion 4 (Objective Tone): Prefer fact-based, neutral language over emotional manipulation.
Paragraph 6 — Conclusion (Call to Action)
Urges readers to exercise critical thinking and perform due diligence to combat misinformation in the digital age.
